conceptName: How a running thing is named
factStatement: Each running process is given a number that identifies it while it runs, and that number is how anything else refers to it.
familyName: Recognising what a process identifier is for
measurementObjective: Given a described situation, say what the identifier refers to and what it does not.
distractorStrategy: The identifier treated as naming the program rather than this run of it; treated as fixed for a program across restarts; treated as a position in a list.
notes: Keep this about the identifier alone. Whether a program differs from a process is the parent skill and is not re-asked.

conceptName: The condition a process is in
factStatement: A process exists in one of several conditions — using the processor, ready and waiting for it, or blocked waiting for something else.
familyName: Naming the condition a described process is in
measurementObjective: Given a description of what a process is doing, name its condition.
distractorStrategy: Waiting for the processor confused with waiting for input, which are different conditions with different remedies; anything not finished called running.
notes: The two kinds of waiting are the whole of this family; a stem that does not distinguish them measures nothing.

factStatement: A process is started by another, which leaves a relationship between them that outlives the starting.
familyName: Recognising that one process started another
measurementObjective: Given a described situation, say which process started which.
distractorStrategy: The relationship read as containment, with the child assumed to run inside the parent; the order reversed; the two treated as unrelated once both are running.

conceptName: The condition a process is in
factStatement: A process changes condition because of a specific event — being given the processor, asking for input, or the input arriving.
familyName: Saying what moved a process between conditions
measurementObjective: Given a process that has changed condition, identify the event responsible.
distractorStrategy: An event named that would cause a different transition; the transition attributed to the process deciding; the direction reversed.

factStatement: A process started in the foreground holds the terminal until it finishes; one in the background does not, and the terminal remains usable.
familyName: Deciding which way a described job was started
measurementObjective: Given a described session, say whether the job holds the terminal and what follows.
distractorStrategy: A background job assumed to produce no output on the terminal, which it may still do; a foreground job assumed to have stopped because the prompt has not returned.
notes: That a background job can still write to the screen is the detail worth an item.

factStatement: A finishing process reports a value saying whether it succeeded, and whatever started it can read that value.
familyName: Reasoning about what a finished process reports
measurementObjective: Given a process that has ended, say what is available afterwards and to whom.
distractorStrategy: The reported value confused with what the process printed; success assumed because output appeared; the value assumed readable by anything rather than by what started it.
notes: Output and result are different channels, and a process can print plenty while reporting failure.

factStatement: A process can be asked to stop, which it may handle and tidy up after, or stopped outright, which it cannot refuse and cannot prepare for.
familyName: Predicting what a request to stop actually does
measurementObjective: Given a request to stop a process, say what the process is able to do about it.
distractorStrategy: Both kinds treated as immediate; the polite request assumed always obeyed; the forced stop assumed to give the process a chance to save.
notes: Unsaved work surviving one and not the other is the consequence that makes this worth measuring.

factStatement: A process whose starter has ended usually keeps running, and is adopted rather than stopped.
familyName: Predicting what happens to a child when its starter ends
measurementObjective: Given a parent that has ended, say what becomes of the process it started.
distractorStrategy: The child assumed to stop with its parent — the intuitive answer and the wrong one; the child assumed to become unreachable; the whole tree assumed to be cleaned up.
notes: A closed terminal leaving a job running is the situation students actually meet.

conceptName: How a running thing is named
factStatement: An identifier belongs to one process at a time and can be given to a different process after the first has ended.
familyName: Reasoning about an identifier recorded earlier
measurementObjective: Given an identifier recorded some time ago, say what can now be concluded from it.
distractorStrategy: The identifier assumed still to name the original process; assumed to name nothing once the original ended; the risk described as theoretical where the stem shows a reuse.
notes: Acting on a stale identifier is how the wrong process gets stopped, which the diagnosis family then picks up.

factStatement: A listing of running processes describes the moment it was taken and may be out of date by the time it is read.
familyName: Reading a described listing of running processes
measurementObjective: Given a described listing, say what it shows and what cannot be concluded from it.
distractorStrategy: A process absent from the listing concluded never to have run; a high figure at one instant read as a sustained condition; the snapshot treated as continuously updating.
notes: Listings are described in words with named columns, since this bank cannot rely on any tool's exact output.

conceptName: When a process will not go
factStatement: A process blocked waiting for something outside itself cannot act on a polite request to stop until the wait ends.
familyName: Diagnosing a process that will not stop when asked
measurementObjective: Given a process ignoring a stop request, identify why and what would work.
distractorStrategy: The process described as having crashed, which would be a different condition; the request assumed not to have been delivered; forcing it proposed without noting what is lost.

conceptName: When a process will not go
factStatement: An action aimed at an identifier that now belongs to something else succeeds, and stops the wrong thing.
familyName: Diagnosing an action that hit the wrong process
measurementObjective: Given an unexpected consequence after stopping a process, decide whether the target was wrong.
distractorStrategy: The original process blamed for side effects; the command reported as having failed, where it reported success; a second unrelated fault proposed.
notes: That the command reports success is the detail that makes this hard and must appear in every stem.

factStatement: What a process leaves behind — files, children, a reported result — depends on how it ended as much as on what it did.
familyName: Reasoning about what a process left behind
measurementObjective: Given how a process ran and ended, say what remains afterwards.
distractorStrategy: Everything assumed cleaned up on exit; nothing assumed cleaned up; a consequence named that depends on how it ended, stated as though it always followed.

factStatement: Whether to ask, to wait, or to force depends on what the process is holding and what would be lost.
familyName: Choosing how to stop a process safely
measurementObjective: Given a process and what it is doing, choose the intervention that meets the requirement.
distractorStrategy: Forcing chosen where the process is mid-write and would leave a corrupt file; waiting chosen where the stem states the wait is unbounded; an intervention aimed at the wrong level.
notes: Every option must be a real intervention, wrong only for the situation described.

factStatement: Identity, condition, a starting relationship and a reported result describe containers, jobs and tasks as well as processes.
familyName: Applying the process model to an unfamiliar runtime
measurementObjective: Given an unfamiliar runtime described in its own terms, answer a question about its behaviour.
distractorStrategy: An answer that would hold if the runtime cleaned up its children, where the stem says otherwise; an answer requiring a property the stem does not grant; the model applied at the wrong level.
notes: The runtime is fully described in the stem and never named, so this measures transfer rather than familiarity.

factStatement: Working memory holds what a program is using now and is lost when it ends; storage holds what survives.
familyName: Deciding which of the two a described thing is in
measurementObjective: Given a described item, say whether it is in working memory or in storage.
distractorStrategy: An opened file assumed to be entirely in memory; a variable assumed to be on disk because the program was loaded from there; the two treated as interchangeable because both hold data.

factStatement: Values belonging to a call live in a region that is released when the call returns; values meant to outlive it live in a region that is not.
familyName: Deciding which region a described value lives in
measurementObjective: Given a described value and how long it is needed, say which region holds it.
distractorStrategy: Size used as the criterion rather than lifetime; every value assumed to live in one region; a value returned from a call assumed to be released with it.
notes: Lifetime rather than size is the rule, and size is the criterion students reach for first.

factStatement: The addresses a program sees are its own, and two programs may hold the same address referring to different physical memory.
familyName: Recognising what an address a program sees refers to
measurementObjective: Given two programs holding the same address, say whether they refer to the same memory.
distractorStrategy: The same address assumed to mean the same location; addresses assumed to be assigned in the order programs start; the address assumed meaningless.
notes: This is the fact that makes isolation intelligible rather than magical, and the parent skill asserts isolation without explaining it.

factStatement: How long a piece of memory lasts is decided by how it was obtained, not by what is stored in it.
familyName: Saying how long a described allocation lasts
measurementObjective: Given a described allocation, say when it is released.
distractorStrategy: Release assumed when the last use passes; release assumed only at program exit; lifetime tied to the size of what is held.

conceptName: What a chain of calls costs
factStatement: Every call in progress holds its own space, so a chain of calls holds space for all of them at once.
familyName: Reasoning about what a chain of calls holds
measurementObjective: Given a described chain of calls, say how much is held and when it is released.
distractorStrategy: Only the innermost call assumed to hold space; space assumed released as each call is entered; the total assumed independent of depth.

factStatement: Memory obtained for an indefinite lifetime stays held until it is released, whether or not anything still uses it.
familyName: Reasoning about memory that is no longer used
measurementObjective: Given memory that is no longer needed, say whether it is available again.
distractorStrategy: Memory assumed reclaimed when the last reference goes, which depends on the language and is stated in the stem; assumed reclaimed at the end of the enclosing call.
notes: Whether the language reclaims automatically must be stated in every stem, or the item has two defensible answers.

factStatement: When programs want more memory than physically exists, some of it is kept in storage and fetched back, which is far slower.
familyName: Predicting what happens when memory is oversubscribed
measurementObjective: Given a machine using more memory than it has, say what is observed.
distractorStrategy: An immediate failure assumed, where slowness comes first; the slowdown attributed to the processor; the borrowing assumed free because it works.
notes: That it gets slow before it fails is the observation that makes memory pressure diagnosable at all.

factStatement: Two programs see separate memory unless something was specifically arranged to let them share.
familyName: Deciding whether two programs see the same memory
measurementObjective: Given two described programs, say whether a change made by one is visible to the other.
distractorStrategy: Sharing assumed because both run on one machine; sharing assumed because both were started from the same program; sharing declared impossible.

factStatement: What a program needs is decided by how much it holds simultaneously, not by how much it processes in total.
familyName: Reasoning about how much memory a task needs
measurementObjective: Given a described task, say what determines the memory it requires.
distractorStrategy: Total data processed offered as the requirement, which is the dominant confusion; the file size offered where the program reads a line at a time; the requirement assumed fixed regardless of approach.
notes: Reading a large file line by line versus loading it whole is the clearest pair and should recur.

factStatement: Exhausting memory shows as a refusal to allocate, as a process being stopped from outside, or as sustained slowness — not usually as a clear message.
familyName: Recognising what running out of memory looks like
measurementObjective: Given described symptoms, say whether memory exhaustion accounts for them.
distractorStrategy: A process disappearing without a message attributed to a crash in its own code; symptoms attributed to memory where the stem points elsewhere, so the family does not teach one answer.

factStatement: Memory rising steadily and never falling means something is being obtained repeatedly and released never.
familyName: Diagnosing memory that only ever rises
measurementObjective: Given a described growth pattern, say what it indicates and what would confirm it.
distractorStrategy: Growth that levels off diagnosed as a leak, which it is not; the fault attributed to load, where the stem holds load constant; restarting proposed as a diagnosis rather than a mitigation.
notes: A pattern that rises and levels off must appear somewhere in the family as a non-fault.

factStatement: A chain of calls with no end exhausts the region reserved for calls, which is much smaller than memory as a whole.
familyName: Diagnosing a failure caused by call depth
measurementObjective: Given a program failing quickly on a small input, decide whether call depth explains it.
distractorStrategy: The failure attributed to the machine being short of memory, where the input is tiny; a leak proposed, which would take time rather than failing at once; the input blamed.
notes: Failing fast on a small input is what separates this from every other memory fault and must be in the stem.

conceptName: Memory as a cause of slowness
factStatement: A machine short of memory becomes slow at everything, because time goes on moving memory rather than on the work.
familyName: Deciding whether memory explains a slowdown
measurementObjective: Given a described slowdown, say whether memory pressure accounts for it and what would confirm it.
distractorStrategy: A slowdown in one program only attributed to memory pressure, which would affect everything; memory ruled out because the processor is busy, when moving memory keeps it busy.

factStatement: Holding something for as long as it might be needed costs memory; obtaining it again each time costs work.
familyName: Choosing where a value should be held
measurementObjective: Given a requirement with stated constraints, choose where and how long to hold a value.
distractorStrategy: Everything held for speed where the stem constrains memory; nothing held where the stem states the recomputation is expensive; a choice that is right in general and wrong under the stated constraint.

factStatement: Obtain, hold, release and exhaust describe connections, handles and locks as well as memory.
familyName: Applying the memory model to another bounded resource
measurementObjective: Given an unfamiliar bounded resource, answer a question about holding and exhausting it.
distractorStrategy: An answer assuming the resource is reclaimed automatically where the stem says otherwise; an answer treating exhaustion as impossible; the model applied to a resource the stem describes as unbounded.
notes: The resource is described in the stem and never named as a database connection or a file handle, so the transfer is the measurement.

factStatement: A path beginning at the top of the tree means the same thing from anywhere; one that does not is read from wherever you happen to be.
familyName: Telling the two kinds of path apart
measurementObjective: Given a written path, say whether its meaning depends on where you are.
distractorStrategy: Length used as the criterion, with long paths assumed absolute; a path starting with a name assumed to start at the top; the distinction made on whether the file exists.
notes: The parent skill asks what a path refers to; this family asks only what kind of path it is, which is the fact the resolution family needs.

conceptName: The three things that may be allowed
factStatement: Reading gets the contents, writing changes them, and running executes the file — three separate permissions that do not imply one another.
familyName: Naming what each permission allows
measurementObjective: Given an action on a file, name the permission it requires.
distractorStrategy: Write assumed to include read; read assumed to include the ability to run; the three treated as levels where each includes the ones below.
notes: That the three are independent rather than ranked is the fact everything else here rests on.

factStatement: Permissions are recorded separately for the owner, for a group and for everyone else, and a user is judged under the first class they fall into.
familyName: Deciding which set of permissions applies to a user
measurementObjective: Given a user and a file, say which of the three sets governs them.
distractorStrategy: The owner assumed to also get the group permissions, so that the most generous set applies; the everyone-else set assumed to apply to everyone including the owner.
notes: That the owner is judged only by the owner set, even when the group set is more generous, is the surprising case.

conceptName: Working out where a path lands
factStatement: A relative path is resolved by joining it to the current directory, so the same path reaches different files from different places.
familyName: Resolving a relative path from a stated directory
measurementObjective: Given a current directory and a relative path, say which file is reached.
distractorStrategy: The path resolved from the top of the tree; resolved from the directory holding the program rather than the current one; a result one level out.
notes: The current directory is stated explicitly in every stem, and the tree is written out, so nothing depends on guessing a layout.

conceptName: Working out where a path lands
factStatement: Every directory contains a name meaning itself and a name meaning the one above it, and those names are used in paths like any other.
familyName: Resolving a path that goes upwards
measurementObjective: Given a path containing a step upwards, say where it lands.
distractorStrategy: Two upward steps treated as one; the upward step applied after the rest of the path rather than in order; the step upward from the top assumed to be an error.

factStatement: Whether an action succeeds is decided by looking up the user class and then the single permission that action needs.
familyName: Deciding whether a described action succeeds
measurementObjective: Given a user, a file and its permissions, say whether the action is allowed.
distractorStrategy: The most generous set applied; a permission checked that the action does not need; the answer resting on ownership where the user is not the owner.

factStatement: On a directory, reading lists the names, writing adds and removes entries, and running permits passing through to what is inside.
familyName: Reasoning about permissions on a directory
measurementObjective: Given a directory and its permissions, say what a user can do with what is inside.
distractorStrategy: Directory permissions read as though the directory were a file; listing assumed to require the same permission as reaching through; a readable directory assumed to make its contents readable.
notes: Being able to reach a known file without being able to list the directory is the case that shows the two apart.

factStatement: Removing a file changes the directory that lists it, so it is the directory permissions that decide, not the file's.
familyName: Deciding whether a file can be removed
measurementObjective: Given a file and its directory with their permissions, say whether the file can be deleted.
distractorStrategy: The file's own write permission consulted — the answer almost everyone gives; ownership of the file treated as decisive; the deletion assumed impossible on a read-only file.
notes: A read-only file in a writable directory is the canonical stem and must appear.

factStatement: A permission summary reads as three groups of three, in the order owner, group, everyone else.
familyName: Reading a described permission summary
measurementObjective: Given a permission summary, say what a named user may do.
distractorStrategy: The groups read in the wrong order, so that everyone-else permissions are attributed to the owner; the three within a group taken in the wrong order; a missing permission read as present.
notes: Summaries are written out in the stem with the order stated, since this bank cannot assume any tool's display.

conceptName: Working out where a path lands
factStatement: Different paths can name the same file, so two paths looking different does not mean two files.
familyName: Deciding whether two paths reach the same file
measurementObjective: Given two paths and a current directory, say whether they reach the same file.
distractorStrategy: Two paths assumed different because they are written differently; assumed the same because they end in the same name; the comparison made without resolving the relative one.

factStatement: An action can be refused because of the file itself or because of a directory anywhere along the way to it.
familyName: Locating what caused an action to be refused
measurementObjective: Given a refused action and the permissions along the path, identify what blocked it.
distractorStrategy: The file blamed where a directory on the way is the obstacle; the wrong directory in the chain named; ownership blamed where the permissions are the obstacle.
notes: A perfectly readable file inside an unreachable directory is the stem this family exists for.

factStatement: A relative path that worked yesterday can fail today because it was resolved from a different directory, not because anything moved.
familyName: Diagnosing a path that resolved from somewhere else
measurementObjective: Given a path that worked and now does not, decide whether the starting directory explains it.
distractorStrategy: The file assumed deleted or moved; permissions blamed, where the stem shows the file is readable from elsewhere; the path declared malformed.
notes: The stem must establish that the file is still there and still readable, or the diagnosis is a guess.

factStatement: Changing a permission changes what a whole class of users may do, including users nobody had in mind.
familyName: Reasoning about who a permission change affects
measurementObjective: Given a proposed permission change, say who gains what.
distractorStrategy: The change assumed to affect only the person it was made for; the reach understated by one class; a change to a directory assumed not to affect what is inside.

factStatement: A requirement is met by the smallest set of permissions that satisfies it, because everything beyond that is granted to people who did not need it.
familyName: Choosing the narrowest permissions that meet a requirement
measurementObjective: Given a stated requirement, choose the permissions that satisfy it without granting more.
distractorStrategy: A grant that works and gives everyone else more than they need; one narrow enough to break the stated requirement; a grant on the file where the requirement turns on the directory.
notes: Every option must satisfy some requirement; only the stated one separates them.

factStatement: An owner, a group, a default and a set of separate permissions describe shared documents and repositories as well as files.
familyName: Applying the access model to an unfamiliar system
measurementObjective: Given an unfamiliar access system described in its own terms, answer a question about what a user may do.
distractorStrategy: The most generous applicable set assumed to apply; permissions assumed to be ranked when the stem describes them as independent; an answer requiring a rule the stem does not state.
notes: The system is described fully in the stem and never named, so this measures the model rather than knowledge of any product.

conceptName: The parts of a command line
factStatement: A command line names what to run, then options that change how it behaves, then the things it acts on.
familyName: Naming the parts of a described command line
measurementObjective: Given a described command line, say which part is the thing being acted on.
distractorStrategy: An option mistaken for a target; the command name counted among its arguments; position assumed to determine role regardless of form.
notes: Parts are described by role rather than by any particular spelling, so nothing here rewards recall of a flag.

factStatement: A command with no path given acts in the current directory, which is a property of the session rather than of the command.
familyName: Recognising where a command will act
measurementObjective: Given a session, say which directory a command with no path affects.
distractorStrategy: The home directory assumed regardless of where the session is; the directory holding the command assumed; the location assumed fixed for the whole session.

factStatement: Each command does one job, and choosing between them is a matter of matching the job rather than of preference.
familyName: Matching a described need to the kind of command that meets it
measurementObjective: Given a described need, say what kind of command answers it.
distractorStrategy: A command that inspects offered where one that changes is needed; one that acts on names offered where contents are meant; copying offered where moving is described.
notes: Commands are described by what they do, never named, so the family survives any shell.

factStatement: Changing directory changes where every later command with no path will act.
familyName: Working out where a sequence of moves ends up
measurementObjective: Given a starting directory and a sequence of moves, say where the session ends.
distractorStrategy: A move treated as relative when it was absolute; upward moves miscounted by one; a failed move assumed to have happened.

factStatement: A plain listing omits entries whose names mark them as hidden, and shows names rather than contents.
familyName: Saying what a listing does and does not include
measurementObjective: Given a described listing, say what is missing from it.
distractorStrategy: An empty listing read as an empty directory; hidden entries assumed not to exist; a listing assumed to show what is inside subdirectories.

factStatement: Copying leaves the original in place and moving does not, and both may overwrite something at the destination.
familyName: Saying what remains after a copy or a move
measurementObjective: Given a described copy or move, say what exists afterwards and where.
distractorStrategy: A move assumed to leave the original; an overwrite at the destination overlooked; a rename treated as producing two files.

factStatement: A pattern selects the existing names that match it, and the command receives those names rather than the pattern.
familyName: Working out which names a pattern selects
measurementObjective: Given a directory and a pattern, say which entries are selected.
distractorStrategy: A pattern assumed to reach inside subdirectories; hidden names assumed to match a general pattern; a name matched that differs in case where the stem states matching is case sensitive.
notes: The directory contents are written out in the stem, so the answer is checkable rather than remembered.

factStatement: Several ordinary commands overwrite or remove without confirming, and there is no recovery afterwards.
familyName: Recognising when a command will destroy something
measurementObjective: Given a command and a described directory, say what would be lost.
distractorStrategy: A confirmation assumed; the loss assumed recoverable from a bin; the destruction understated by one file.

factStatement: A command told to work throughout a tree reaches everything below the named directory, however deep.
familyName: Working out how far a command through a tree reaches
measurementObjective: Given a tree and a command that works throughout it, say what is affected.
distractorStrategy: Only the immediate contents assumed affected; only directories assumed affected; the named directory itself excluded.
notes: The tree is written out in the stem to a stated depth, so counting what is affected is possible.

factStatement: A name containing a space is read as two separate things unless it is quoted.
familyName: Predicting what a command receives for an awkward name
measurementObjective: Given a name with a space or an unusual character, say what the command receives.
distractorStrategy: The name assumed to arrive whole; the command assumed to fail rather than to act on two things; quoting assumed unnecessary because the name exists.
notes: Acting on two wrong things rather than failing is what makes this dangerous and is the answer worth measuring.

conceptName: When a command cannot find its target
factStatement: A command reporting that something does not exist is usually right about the place it looked and wrong about where you thought it was looking.
familyName: Diagnosing a command that cannot find its target
measurementObjective: Given a not-found result and a described session, identify why.
distractorStrategy: The file assumed deleted; a permission problem proposed, which reports differently; the name assumed misspelled where the stem shows it matches.

conceptName: When a command cannot find its target
factStatement: A pattern that matched more names than intended produces a command that succeeds on all of them.
familyName: Diagnosing a pattern that selected too much
measurementObjective: Given an unexpected outcome after using a pattern, identify what it matched.
distractorStrategy: The command blamed rather than the pattern; the overmatch located in the wrong part of the pattern; the outcome attributed to a second command.

factStatement: A destructive command can usually be preceded by one that shows exactly what it would act on.
familyName: Choosing how to establish what a command would affect
measurementObjective: Given a risky command, choose the step that would show its reach before it runs.
distractorStrategy: Running it and watching, which is not a check; a check that lists something other than what the command would act on; taking a backup, which mitigates rather than establishes.
notes: Backing up is a reasonable habit and a wrong answer here, since the question asks what would be affected.

factStatement: Whether to copy or move, act on one thing or many, and act here or throughout a tree is settled by the requirement rather than by habit.
familyName: Choosing the command that meets a stated requirement
measurementObjective: Given a requirement, choose the command that satisfies it without doing more.
distractorStrategy: A command that meets the requirement and also destroys something not mentioned; one that reaches further than asked; one that would work if the target were a single file.

factStatement: A command nobody has seen before is read by identifying its options and its targets and asking what it would act on.
familyName: Reading an unfamiliar command safely
measurementObjective: Given an unfamiliar command described by its documented behaviour, say what it would do here.
distractorStrategy: An answer requiring behaviour the description does not state; the target and an option confused; an answer that would hold if the command acted only on the immediate directory.
notes: The command is invented and its behaviour fully described, so this measures reading rather than recall.

factStatement: A command reads from one channel and writes to two — ordinary output and errors — and the two outgoing channels are separate.
familyName: Naming the channel a described thing travels on
measurementObjective: Given a described piece of output, say which channel carries it.
distractorStrategy: Errors assumed to travel with ordinary output because both appear on the screen; the incoming channel confused with an argument; a warning assumed to be ordinary output.
notes: That errors and output share a screen and not a channel is the fact the whole skill rests on.

factStatement: Output can be sent to a file instead of the screen, and doing so removes it from the screen entirely.
familyName: Saying where redirected output ends up
measurementObjective: Given a command with its output redirected, say what appears where.
distractorStrategy: Output assumed to appear both on screen and in the file; errors assumed to follow ordinary output into the file; the file assumed to be created only if output occurs.

factStatement: A pipe connects the ordinary output of one command to the incoming channel of the next, and carries nothing else.
familyName: Recognising what a pipe connects
measurementObjective: Given two commands joined by a pipe, say what the second receives.
distractorStrategy: The second command assumed to receive the first as an argument; errors assumed to travel down the pipe; the pipe assumed to run the two commands one after the other with no connection.

factStatement: Each stage sees only what the stage before it produced, and nothing of what that stage was given.
familyName: Working out what a later stage receives
measurementObjective: Given a pipeline, say what the final stage is working on.
distractorStrategy: The final stage assumed to see the original input; assumed to see the output of every earlier stage; a filtering stage assumed to pass everything on.

factStatement: Redirecting output either replaces what a file held or adds to the end of it, and the two are written differently.
familyName: Saying what a file holds after a redirection
measurementObjective: Given a file with contents and a redirection into it, say what it holds afterwards.
distractorStrategy: Replacement assumed to add; addition assumed to replace; the file assumed to be left alone when the command produced no output, where it is still emptied.
notes: A file emptied by a command that produced nothing is the case worth an item, and the one that loses real data.

factStatement: Redirecting or piping ordinary output leaves errors going to the screen, because they travel on the other channel.
familyName: Saying where errors appear in a redirected command
measurementObjective: Given a command whose output is redirected, say where its errors appear.
distractorStrategy: Errors assumed to follow output into the file — the dominant expectation; errors assumed suppressed entirely; errors assumed to stop the pipeline.

factStatement: A chain of filters applies each in turn, so the result depends on all of them and on their order.
familyName: Working out what a chain of filters produces
measurementObjective: Given stated input and a chain of described filters, say what emerges.
distractorStrategy: The stages applied in the wrong order; one stage skipped; the result of applying each stage to the original input rather than to its predecessor.
notes: Input is written out in the stem and filters described by behaviour, so the answer is derivable rather than remembered.

factStatement: A stage that counts reports what arrived at it, which is what earlier stages let through rather than what existed originally.
familyName: Saying what a counting stage has counted
measurementObjective: Given a pipeline ending in a count, say what the number refers to.
distractorStrategy: The count read as the size of the original input; read as the number of stages; read as counting matches where the stage counts lines.

factStatement: A stage cannot tell what produced its input or what will consume its output, and behaves the same either way.
familyName: Reasoning about what a stage can and cannot know
measurementObjective: Given a pipeline, say what a named stage has access to.
distractorStrategy: A stage assumed to know the filename its input came from; assumed to know how many stages follow; assumed to change behaviour when its output is redirected.
notes: This independence is what makes composition work and is worth measuring directly rather than assuming.

factStatement: A command can be given a file as its incoming channel, which is not the same as being given the filename as an argument.
familyName: Distinguishing a file supplied as input from one named as an argument
measurementObjective: Given two ways of supplying a file, say how the command sees each.
distractorStrategy: The two treated as identical, which they are for many commands and not all; the command assumed to know the filename in both cases; the difference described as one of efficiency.
notes: That the command can name the file in one case and not the other is the observable difference and should decide the stems.

factStatement: A pipeline producing nothing has one stage that let nothing through, and which one can be established by stopping earlier.
familyName: Locating the stage that produced nothing
measurementObjective: Given a pipeline producing no output, identify how to find the stage responsible.
distractorStrategy: The last stage blamed because it produced the empty result; the input assumed empty where the stem shows otherwise; rewriting the whole pipeline proposed instead of locating the stage.

factStatement: An error seen on the screen while output went to a file is absent from the file, because the two travelled on different channels.
familyName: Diagnosing an error that did not reach the log
measurementObjective: Given output captured to a file with an error missing from it, explain why.
distractorStrategy: The error assumed not to have occurred; the file assumed to have been overwritten; the command assumed to have suppressed the message.
notes: A log that captured everything except the reason for the failure is the situation this exists to explain.

factStatement: Filtering before transforming and transforming before filtering generally give different results, because each stage sees a different thing.
familyName: Reasoning about the effect of reordering stages
measurementObjective: Given a pipeline and a proposed reordering, say whether the result changes and why.
distractorStrategy: Order assumed never to matter; order assumed always to matter, where two stages genuinely commute; the change described in the wrong direction.
notes: One stem must use a pair that genuinely commutes, so the family does not teach that order always matters.

factStatement: What the pipeline must produce settles which stages are needed and what order they go in.
familyName: Choosing the pipeline that meets a requirement
measurementObjective: Given a requirement, choose the pipeline that produces exactly what is wanted.
distractorStrategy: A pipeline correct except for the order of two stages; one that discards the errors the requirement asks to keep; one that produces the right content in the wrong quantity.

factStatement: Small pieces joined so that each consumes what the last produced describes data pipelines and processing chains as well as shell commands.
familyName: Applying composition to an unfamiliar set of tools
measurementObjective: Given an unfamiliar system of composable stages, answer a question about what a chain produces.
distractorStrategy: An answer assuming a later stage can see the original input; one assuming stages run independently rather than in sequence; one requiring a stage to know its position.
notes: The system is described in the stem and is never a shell, so the transfer is what is measured.
